An electron accelerated through a potential difference \(V\) gains kinetic energy \(eV\). The X-ray photon of highest frequency is the one produced when the whole of this energy is converted into a single photon, so \(h\nu_{\max} = eV\).

Energy of the electron: \(E = eV = (1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C})(30 \times 10^{3}\,\text{V}) = 4.8 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{J}\).

(a) \(\nu_{\max} = \dfrac{E}{h} = \dfrac{4.8 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{J}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}} = 7.24 \times 10^{18}\,\text{Hz}\)

(b) \(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{c}{\nu_{\max}} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{7.24 \times 10^{18}\,\text{Hz}} = 4.14 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\)

(a) \(\nu_{\max} = 7.24 \times 10^{18}\,\text{Hz}\)
(b) \(\lambda_{\min} = 4.14 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m} \approx 0.041\,\text{nm}\)

Einstein's photoelectric equation gives \(K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi_0\).

Energy of an incident photon: \(h\nu = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(6 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}) = 3.978 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = \dfrac{3.978 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}\,\text{eV} = 2.49\,\text{eV}\)

(a) \(K_{\max} = 2.49\,\text{eV} - 2.14\,\text{eV} = 0.35\,\text{eV} = 5.54 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J}\)

(b) The stopping potential satisfies \(eV_0 = K_{\max}\), so numerically \(V_0 = 0.35\,\text{V}\).

(c) From \(K_{\max} = \tfrac{1}{2} m v_{\max}^{2}\),
\(v_{\max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K_{\max}}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 5.54 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}}} = 3.49 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

(a) \(K_{\max} = 0.35\,\text{eV}\)
(b) \(V_0 = 0.35\,\text{V}\)
(c) \(v_{\max} = 3.49 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1} \approx 349\,\text{km s}^{-1}\)

The cut-off (stopping) potential is the retarding potential that just stops the fastest photoelectron, so the work done against it equals the maximum kinetic energy:
\(K_{\max} = eV_0\)

\(K_{\max} = (1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C})(1.5\,\text{V}) = 2.4 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

\(K_{\max} = 1.5\,\text{eV} = 2.4 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

Take \(\lambda = 632.8\,\text{nm} = 632.8 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}\) and \(P = 9.42\,\text{mW} = 9.42 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{W}\).

(a) Photon energy \(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1})}{632.8 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 3.14 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 1.96\,\text{eV}\)
Photon momentum \(p = \dfrac{E}{c} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}}{632.8 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 1.05 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)

(b) Since the beam is narrower than the target, every photon emitted arrives at the target, so the arrival rate is
\(N = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{9.42 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{W}}{3.14 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}} = 3.0 \times 10^{16}\) photons per second.

(c) A hydrogen atom of mass \(m_H = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}\) has the same momentum when
\(v = \dfrac{p}{m_H} = \dfrac{1.05 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}}{1.66 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}} = 0.63\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

(a) \(E = 3.14 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\ (= 1.96\,\text{eV})\), \(p = 1.05 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)
(b) \(N = 3.0 \times 10^{16}\) photons per second
(c) \(v = 0.63\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Einstein's equation written for the stopping potential is
\(V_0 = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\)
so the graph of cut-off voltage against frequency is a straight line of slope \(h/e\).

Hence \(h = (\text{slope}) \times e = (4.12 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{V s})(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C})\)

\(h = 6.59 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\)

The stopping (cut-off) potential satisfies \(eV_0 = K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi_0 = h(\nu - \nu_0)\), since \(\phi_0 = h\nu_0\).

\(eV_0 = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})\left(8.2 \times 10^{14} - 3.3 \times 10^{14}\right)\,\text{Hz}\)
\(= (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(4.9 \times 10^{14})\,\text{J} = 3.25 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

\(V_0 = \dfrac{3.25 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}} = 2.03\,\text{V}\)

Cut-off voltage \(V_0 = 2.03\,\text{V}\)

Photoemission occurs only if the incident photon carries at least the work function, i.e. only if \(\lambda \le \lambda_0\) where \(\lambda_0 = hc/\phi_0\) is the threshold wavelength.

Threshold wavelength: \(\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1})}{4.2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}} = 2.96 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 296\,\text{nm}\)

The incident radiation has \(\lambda = 330\,\text{nm} > \lambda_0\). Equivalently, its photon energy is
\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}\,\text{J m}}{330 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 6.03 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 3.77\,\text{eV}\), which is less than the work function \(4.2\,\text{eV}\).

No. The metal will not give photoelectric emission at \(330\,\text{nm}\), because \(3.77\,\text{eV} < 4.2\,\text{eV}\) (the threshold wavelength is \(296\,\text{nm}\)).

By Einstein's photoelectric equation, \(h\nu = \phi_0 + K_{\max} = h\nu_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^{2}\).

Maximum kinetic energy:
\(K_{\max} = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg})(6.0 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1})^{2} = 1.64 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

Hence \(h\nu_0 = h\nu - K_{\max} = (6.63 \times 10^{-34})(7.21 \times 10^{14}) - 1.64 \times 10^{-19}\)
\(= 4.78 \times 10^{-19} - 1.64 \times 10^{-19} = 3.14 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

\(\nu_0 = \dfrac{3.14 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}} = 4.74 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\)

Threshold frequency \(\nu_0 = 4.74 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\)

From Einstein's equation, \(\phi_0 = h\nu - eV_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - eV_0\).

Photon energy: \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1})}{488 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 4.08 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 2.55\,\text{eV}\)

Energy carried away by the fastest photoelectron: \(eV_0 = 0.38\,\text{eV}\).

\(\phi_0 = 2.55\,\text{eV} - 0.38\,\text{eV} = 2.17\,\text{eV}\)

Work function \(\phi_0 = 2.17\,\text{eV}\ (= 3.47 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J})\)

[Textbook misprint in the answer key: part (c) is printed as \(3.0 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{m}\), which is too large by a factor of \(100\) — the de Broglie wavelength of the dust particle is \(3.0 \times 10^{-25}\,\text{m}\). Parts (a) and (b) are printed correctly, and they are what settle it: the key's own (b) gives \(\lambda = 1.1 \times 10^{-32}\,\text{m}\) at \(p = 0.060\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\), i.e. \(h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\), and that same \(h\) at \(p = 2.2 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) returns exactly \(3.0 \times 10^{-25}\,\text{m}\) — reproducing the key's own mantissa \(3.0\) with only the exponent differing. A mass of \(1.005 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{kg}\) would be needed to make \(3.0 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{m}\) correct, two decades away from the \(1.0 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{kg}\) the question states. Only the exponent is broken; the method and the mantissa the book prints are right.] The de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}\), with \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\).

(a) \(p = (0.040\,\text{kg})(1.0 \times 10^{3}\,\text{m s}^{-1}) = 40\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)
\(\lambda = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{40} = 1.66 \times 10^{-35}\,\text{m}\)

(b) \(p = (0.060\,\text{kg})(1.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}) = 0.060\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)
\(\lambda = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{0.060} = 1.11 \times 10^{-32}\,\text{m}\)

(c) \(p = (1.0 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{kg})(2.2\,\text{m s}^{-1}) = 2.2 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)
\(\lambda = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2.2 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.01 \times 10^{-25}\,\text{m}\)

All three are far too small to be measured, which is why macroscopic bodies show no wave behaviour.

(a) \(1.66 \times 10^{-35}\,\text{m}\)
(b) \(1.11 \times 10^{-32}\,\text{m}\)
(c) \(3.01 \times 10^{-25}\,\text{m}\)

Let the electromagnetic radiation have frequency \(\nu\) and wavelength \(\lambda\), so that \(\lambda = c/\nu\).

Each quantum (photon) of this radiation carries energy \(E = h\nu\). A photon is massless and travels at \(c\), so its energy and momentum are related by \(E = pc\). Hence its momentum is
\(p = \dfrac{E}{c} = \dfrac{h\nu}{c} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\)

The de Broglie wavelength of that photon is
\(\lambda_{\text{dB}} = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{h/\lambda} = \lambda\)

So the de Broglie wavelength of the quantum equals the wavelength of the radiation itself, \(\lambda_{\text{dB}} = \lambda\). (This is the content of Eq. (11.7): \(h/p = c/\nu = \lambda\).)
